His intelligence and personality, though different from hers, would have met all her hopes. Their marriage would have helped them both. Her relaxed, lively nature might have softened his thinking and improved his manners. His good judgment, knowledge, and experience of life would have helped her in even more important ways.

But no such happy marriage could now show an admiring world what married happiness truly meant. A very different wedding would soon take place in their family, making the other impossible.

She could not imagine how Wickham and Lydia would earn enough to live with reasonable independence. It was easy, though, to imagine how little lasting happiness there could be for two people brought together only because their desires were stronger than their principles.

Mr. Gardiner soon wrote another letter to his brother. He briefly answered Mr. Bennet's thanks, assuring him that he was always eager to help any member of the family. He finished by asking that the matter never be mentioned to him again. The main news in his letter was that Mr. Wickham had decided to leave the militia.

"I very much hoped he would do so," he added, "once the marriage was settled. I think you will agree that leaving that unit is wise, for both his sake and my niece's. Mr. Wickham intends to join the regular army. Some of his old friends are still able and willing to help him with his military career. He has been promised a junior officer's position as an ensign in General----'s regiment, which is now based in the north. Being so far from this part of the country is an advantage. He makes good promises, and I hope they will both behave more carefully among new people, where each will have a reputation to protect. I have written to Colonel Forster, explaining our plans and asking him to assure the people Mr. Wickham owes money to in and around Brighton that they will soon be paid. I have guaranteed payment myself. Would you give the same assurances to his creditors in Meryton? I will attach a list based on the information he has provided. He has reported all his debts; at least, I hope he has not deceived us. Haggerston has our instructions, and everything will be finished in a week. They will then go to his regiment unless you invite them to Longbourn first. Mrs. Gardiner tells me that my niece is very eager to see all of you before she leaves the south.

But it's remarkable that she always hears Jane better than she hears me. Jane speaks so clearly! Still, she won't find her grandmother's hearing any worse than it was two years ago, which is saying a great deal at my mother's age. It really has been two whole years since Jane was here, you know. We've never gone so long without seeing her before. As I told Mrs. Cole, we'll hardly know how to show her enough affection now."

"Are you expecting Miss Fairfax to visit soon?"

"Oh yes, next week."

"Really? That must make you very happy."

"Thank you. You're very kind. Yes, next week. Everyone is so surprised, and everyone says such lovely things. I'm sure she'll be just as happy to see her Highbury friends as they will be to see her. Friday or Saturday, yes. She can't say which, because Colonel Campbell will need the carriage himself on one of those days. It's so kind of them to send her all the way! But they always do, you know. Yes, next Friday or Saturday. That's what her letter is about. That's why she's written outside her usual schedule, as we call it. Normally we wouldn't have heard from her before next Tuesday or Wednesday."

"Yes, that's what I thought. I was afraid I had very little chance of hearing news of Miss Fairfax today."

"How thoughtful of you! No, we wouldn't have heard without this special reason, her coming so soon. My mother is delighted! Jane will stay with us for at least three months. Three months—she says so quite definitely, as I'll have the pleasure of reading to you. You see, the Campbells are going to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon has persuaded her parents to come and see her right away. They hadn't planned to go until summer, but she's so eager to see them again. Until her marriage last October, she'd never been away from them for even a week. It must feel very strange to be in separate kingdoms, I was going to say—well, separate countries, anyway. So she wrote a most urgent letter to her mother, or perhaps her father. I really don't know which, but we'll find out in Jane's letter shortly. She wrote for Mr. Dixon as well as herself, begging them to come immediately. They would meet her parents in Dublin and take them back to their country home, Baly-craig. I imagine it's a beautiful place.

He mounted a spirited horse, the same one that had carried him to victory in Greece, and drove himself into exhaustion through numbing exercise, drowning his troubled thoughts in physical sensation.

Gradually he regained control. At last, like a man recovering from poison, he raised his head above the fumes of fever and passion into the clear air of calm thought. He considered what he should do. First he was struck by how much time had passed while madness, rather than reason, directed his behaviour. A month had gone by without his seeing Evadne. Her influence, rooted in few of his heart's lasting feelings, had greatly weakened. He was no longer her slave, no longer her lover. He would never see her again. By returning wholly to Perdita, he would earn her trust.

Yet even as he made that decision, his imagination pictured the Greek girl's miserable home. Out of noble principle, she had refused to exchange it for more luxurious surroundings. He remembered the splendour of her position and appearance when they first met, her life at Constantinople amid every form of Eastern magnificence. Then he thought of her present poverty, her daily labour, her loneliness, and her faded, hunger-worn face. Compassion filled him. He would visit her once more and devise a way to restore her place in society and the privileges of her rank. Their separation would follow naturally afterward.

He also remembered how, throughout that long month, he had avoided Perdita, fleeing from her as though from the accusations of his conscience. But now he had awakened. He would put everything right, and his future devotion would erase the memory of this one stain upon their peaceful life. The thought cheered him. Calmly and firmly, he mapped out his course. He remembered promising Perdita that he would attend a celebration in his honour that very evening, October 19, the anniversary of his election as Protector. Let the occasion be a hopeful sign of happiness in the years ahead. First he would call briefly on Evadne. He would not linger, but he owed her some explanation, some compensation for his long absence without warning. Then he would return to Perdita, to the world he had forgotten, to social duties, the splendour of rank, and the pleasures of power.

After the scene described in the preceding pages, Perdita had anticipated a complete change in Raymond's manner and behaviour. She expected open communication and a return to the affectionate companionship that had brought such joy to her life.
